items.prompt: What is "black politics" as this unit defines it?
choices: Political tactics that advance someone's position at another person's expense, typically through concealment, deception, or deniability
Any attempt to influence a decision at work, regardless of method
Formal disciplinary action taken by HR against an employee
A negotiation tactic used exclusively in salary discussions
items.explanation: Black politics is specifically defined by concealment/deception at someone else's expense — not by influence-seeking in general, HR action, or salary negotiation.
items.reference:
White politics

Transparent, advances shared goals

Black politics

Hidden, advances one person at another's expense

Why: the dividing line is transparency — could the move survive being stated openly, or does it depend on concealment to work?
items.learnMore:
White vs. black politics

Both involve trying to influence an outcome. What separates them isn't influence-seeking itself.

White politicsBlack politics
Could it survive being said openly?YesNo — depends on concealment
Who benefitsShared goalsOne person, at another's expense
ExampleBuilding a strong case and presenting it clearlyLetting people believe someone else's idea was yours

Common mistake

Assuming any attempt to influence a decision counts as black politics. Every functioning workplace involves influence-seeking — the test is transparency, not whether influence was attempted at all.

items.prompt: How does this unit relate "black" politics to the earlier "white" politics unit in this track?

Black politics is described as simply a more aggressive version of white politics with no other difference
The unit states white politics no longer applies once black politics tactics are present
items.explanation: L1 explicitly frames black politics as the counterpart to white politics — self-serving and often hidden, versus transparent and shared-goal-advancing.

items.prompt: What is "credit-stealing"?
choices: Presenting someone else's work, analysis, or idea as your own, or allowing others to believe it's yours without correcting them
Asking a colleague for feedback on a shared project
Formally requesting a raise based on recent accomplishments
Publicly thanking a teammate for their contribution to a project
items.explanation: Credit-stealing specifically means claiming or allowing false claim to someone else's work — not feedback requests, raise negotiations, or genuine public credit.
items.reference:
🧑‍💻 Claiming — or letting others believe — someone else's work is yours
🤷 Low-risk for the person doing it: it's deniable ("I didn't mean to leave you out")

Why: deniability is what makes credit-stealing common — it's hard to prove intent from a single ambiguous moment.
items.learnMore:
What counts as credit-stealing
SituationCredit-stealing?
"Here's the approach I came up with" over someone else's work, knowing whose it wasYes — active authorship claim
Presenting shared work with no names mentioned at allAmbiguous — could be an oversight
"Here's what [name] built, and why it matters"No — credit given

Its low risk comes from deniability, not from being hard to notice — the room usually sees exactly what happened; what's hard is proving it was deliberate.

Common mistake

Treating 'low-risk for the person doing it' as 'harmless.' Low-risk refers to how hard it is to prove and punish — it still costs the original contributor real, visible credit in the room that matters most.

Because it never actually damages the relationship between colleagues
items.explanation: L1 identifies deniability specifically as what makes credit-stealing low-risk — not legality, policy gaps, or an absence of relationship damage.

items.prompt: What is "scapegoating"?
choices: Deliberately directing blame for a shared or someone else's failure onto a person who wasn't actually responsible for it
Publicly acknowledging your own mistake in a project retrospective
Assigning a task to a specific team member based on their skill set
Reviewing a colleague's code and pointing out a genuine bug they introduced
items.explanation: Scapegoating specifically means misdirecting blame onto someone not actually responsible — not honest self-accountability, task assignment, or legitimate code review.
items.reference:
Credit-stealing

Takes someone else's success as your own

Scapegoating

Puts your (or a shared) failure onto someone else

Why: both move credit or blame away from where it actually belongs — one in each direction.
items.learnMore:
Two tactics, opposite direction
Credit-stealingScapegoating
MovesCredit, toward selfBlame, away from self
TargetSomeone's successSomeone not responsible for a failure
Visible inOften a single clear momentUsually needs a pattern over time

Common mistake

Assuming honest, mistaken blame ('I genuinely thought it was their call') is the same as scapegoating. The definition requires directing blame onto someone deliberately — a good-faith misread of who was responsible isn't the same tactic, even if the outcome looks similar.

items.prompt: Per L2, does recognizing scapegoating typically require different evidence than recognizing credit-stealing?
choices: Yes — scapegoating usually requires noticing a pattern over time, while credit-stealing is often visible in a single specific moment
No — both require identical evidence in every case
Yes, but only because scapegoating is illegal and credit-stealing is not
No — neither tactic can ever be recognized with any confidence
items.explanation: L2 explicitly distinguishes the evidence needed: credit-stealing often shows up in one clear moment, while scapegoating usually needs a pattern to be visible.
items.reference:
Credit-stealing

Often visible in one specific moment

Scapegoating

Usually needs a pattern over time to be distinguishable from an honest misassignment

Why: a single claim of authorship is already a strong signal; a single instance of misplaced blame is still plausibly an honest, mistaken read.
items.learnMore:
Same category, different evidence bar
TacticWhat one incident tells youWhat you usually still need
Credit-stealingA specific claim, in a specific meeting, can already be tellingRepetition, to move from 'telling' to 'proven'
ScapegoatingCould plausibly be a genuine, mistaken read of who was responsibleA pattern — the same blame-shifting, repeated

Common mistake

Applying the same evidence bar to every black-politics tactic. 'This happened once, so I can't act yet' is the right call for scapegoating but too cautious for a clear authorship claim like credit-stealing.

items.prompt: What is "manufactured urgency"?
choices: Falsely framing a request or decision as more time-critical than it actually is, typically to bypass normal scrutiny
A genuinely urgent production incident that requires an immediate response
A project deadline set by a client contract
A calendar reminder set for an upcoming meeting
items.explanation: Manufactured urgency is specifically about falsely inflated time pressure used to avoid scrutiny — not genuine incidents, contractual deadlines, or ordinary reminders.
items.reference:
⏱️ Falsely framing something as more time-critical than it is
🚫 Purpose: bypass normal scrutiny before objections can form

Why: compressing the review window is the whole point — it works by denying people time to think, not by being a good argument.
items.learnMore:
Genuine urgency vs. manufactured urgency
Genuine urgencyManufactured urgency
SourceA real incident or external deadlineInvented or exaggerated by the person pushing it
Effect on scrutinyScrutiny happens fast, not skippedScrutiny is the thing being avoided
Who benefits from the rushWhoever needs the problem solvedThe person pushing the decision through

Common mistake

Treating every fast-moving decision as manufactured urgency. A real production incident or a hard client deadline is genuine time pressure — the tactic is specifically about pressure invented to dodge review, not all pressure.

items.prompt: Why would someone use manufactured urgency as a black-politics tactic?
choices: To push a decision through before objections can form or normal scrutiny can be applied
To give colleagues more time to carefully review a proposal
To comply with a legally mandated deadline
To publicly demonstrate strong project management skills
items.explanation: The tactic's purpose is specifically to compress the window for scrutiny and objection — the opposite of giving more review time or following a legitimate deadline.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what does "sabotage" specifically involve?
choices: Deliberately undermining someone else's work or standing, often while appearing supportive
Openly and publicly criticizing a colleague's proposal in a team meeting
Declining to collaborate on a project due to a scheduling conflict
Reporting a genuine ethics violation through official channels
items.explanation: Sabotage specifically involves undermining someone while maintaining an appearance of support — not open criticism, scheduling conflicts, or legitimate reporting.
items.reference:
SabotageUndermines someone's work while appearing supportive
Weaponized rumorsUnverified/false info, source hidden, to damage reputation

Why: each of the five tactics damages trust through a different mechanism, so recognizing which one is happening changes what evidence to look for.

items.prompt: Per L2, why don't more people confront credit-stealing directly when it happens?

items.explanation: L2 identifies built-in deniability as the specific reason direct confrontation feels risky — not rarity, policy, or self-evidence.
items.reference:

Privately raise it, start documenting

Established pattern

Why: deniability makes one incident genuinely hard to call out publicly, but a repeated pattern can no longer claim 'I didn't know.'
items.learnMore:
Why deniability blocks direct confrontation
SituationAvailable excuseRight-sized response
First, ambiguous instance"I didn't mean to leave you out" — plausiblePrivately raise it, document

A public accusation on a single deniable incident risks making the person raising it look petty or paranoid, even when their read is correct.

Response to the private questionPoints toward
Real apology, visible correctionA lapse, not intent
Verifiable confusion about who was presentingNeeds cleanup, but not necessarily intent
Evasive answer, anger that you noticed, or a repeatPattern much harder to dismiss

Asking privately keeps the door open for a legitimate explanation while making clear the behavior was noticed.

Common mistake

Treating the in-meeting correction as the end of the process. It fixes the room's impression in the moment but doesn't answer whether this was one-time or a pattern — that's what the private conversation is for.

items.prompt: Per L3's "what generalizes" section, does the core lesson about calibrating response to evidence strength apply only to credit-stealing?
choices: No — it generalizes to the other four black-politics tactics from L2's table, not just credit-stealing
Yes — the lesson is stated to apply exclusively to credit-stealing and no other tactic
No, but only to tactics that happen in front of leadership specifically
Yes, but only within engineering teams specifically
items.explanation: L3 explicitly extends the core lesson (calibrating response to whether it's one incident or a pattern) beyond credit-stealing to the other tactics.
items.reference:
Credit-stealing fix

Re-attach your name to work: "since I built that model"

Scapegoating fix

Re-attach the decision to the facts: "I implemented it, I didn't decide to ship it"

Why: the calibration principle (incident vs. pattern) generalizes across tactics; the exact correcting move doesn't.
items.learnMore:
What generalizes, what's tactic-specific
TacticThe 'just restate the fact' correction
Credit-stealingAttach your name back to the work
ScapegoatingAttach the decision back to who actually made it
Sabotage / weaponized rumorsNo single clean factual restatement — these need their own, differently-shaped response

What carries over: calibrate to incident-vs-pattern strength, and don't conflate overreacting with ignoring a real pattern. What doesn't: the exact words of any one correction.

Common mistake

Assuming one scripted line works for every black-politics tactic. The calibration principle generalizes; the specific correcting phrase is shaped around credit-stealing's particular mechanism and doesn't transfer as-is.

items.prompt: Per L3, would the exact in-meeting line ("happy to walk through the assumptions, since I built that model") work equally well for responding to scapegoating?
choices: No — that specific move only works for credit-stealing, where the fix is re-attaching a name to existing work; scapegoating needs a differently-shaped response
Yes — the exact same line works identically for any black-politics tactic
Yes, but only if the word "model" is replaced with "decision"
No, because that line only works in written communication, never spoken aloud
items.explanation: L3 explicitly notes the specific move is shaped for credit-stealing's particular mechanism and doesn't transfer directly to a tactic like scapegoating.
